name: The Tartarean Eye

detectability.signature: A rhythmic bass groan in spacetime itself, felt in hull plating long before instruments confirm contact

proximity: Navigation systems disagree on velocity and heading by widening margins
Chronometers fall seconds behind fleet standard time
contact: Tidal shear stresses hull frames beyond design tolerance
Signal latency stretches; transmissions arrive deepened and slowed
prolonged_exposure: Progressive spaghettification of the vessel along the radial axis
Irrecoverable loss of ship and crew beyond the event horizon

phenomena: Light bending into a luminous ring around the black shadow
Gravitational lensing smearing background galaxies across the rim
Time dilation effects observable near the boundary
hazards: Complete ship destruction inside the event horizon
opportunities: Unmatched research opportunity for gravitational physics
Data valuable to scientific institutions as a natural calibration standard
known_incidents: The Kessler Line lost three ore barges on identical approach vectors within a single decade
Guild navigator Elara Voss returned from a survey run insisting she had watched her own rescue from beyond the dark
description: A perfect circle of absolute darkness, twelve solar masses compressed behind an event horizon barely sixty kilometers wide. The Eye betrays itself only by what it distorts: starlight smears into a luminous corona as background galaxies bend around its rim. Long-range sensors register it as a rhythmic groan in spacetime itself, a bass note felt in hull plating before any instrument confirms it.

The anomaly holds station with geological patience, its accretion disk thin enough that it glows dimly rather than blazing. Ships entering the approach corridor report instruments disagreeing about their own velocity by whole percentages. At the photon sphere, time runs visibly slow; a vessel observed crossing the threshold appears to freeze forever at the edge.

Chartered miners found the Eye four centuries ago when three ore barges vanished along an identical trajectory line. The subsequent survey cost the cartographic guild both its probes and its chief navigator, who returned insisting she had watched her own rescue from the far side of the dark. It remains the most precisely measured singularity in recorded space.

Today the Eye serves as a calibration standard for gravitational instrumentation and a graveyard marker for the careless. Research enclaves maintain permanent stations at the outermost stable orbit, harvesting data no laboratory can replicate. Every pilot charts around it; every physicist dreams about it.
